title: Orientation Test (CCW)
description: The single primitive that tells you which way three points turn

blocks.text: The orientation test is the most important primitive in computational geometry. Given three points, it tells you whether the path through them turns left, turns right, or goes straight.
From this one test you can build segment intersection, convex hull, polygon area, and point in polygon checks. If you learn only one geometry tool, make it this one.
Imagine walking from point A to point B and then on to point C. At B you either turn left, turn right, or keep going straight. That turning direction is the orientation of the three points.

blocks.caption: Three points can turn left (CCW), turn right (CW), or go straight (collinear)

blocks.text: A left turn is called counter-clockwise, or CCW. A right turn is clockwise, or CW. Going straight means the three points are collinear.
To find the orientation, take the cross product of the vector from A to B with the vector from A to C. This single expression captures the turn direction.

blocks.caption: The sign of the cross product tells you the orientation directly

blocks.text: We never even care about the actual value, only its sign. That is what makes the test so clean and so fast.
The sign of that cross product maps directly to the three cases.

items: Positive: the turn is counter-clockwise, a left turn
Negative: the turn is clockwise, a right turn
Zero: the three points are collinear

blocks.text:
Sign conventions vary:

Whether positive means left or right depends on the axis convention. Pick one and stay consistent; what matters is comparing signs, not the labels.
The whole test is one expression and a sign check. Using integer coordinates keeps it exact.

codes.python:
def orientation(a, b, c):
    v = (b[0]-a[0]) * (c[1]-a[1]) - (b[1]-a[1]) * (c[0]-a[0])
    if v > 0: return 1     # counter-clockwise, left turn
    if v < 0: return -1    # clockwise, right turn
    return 0               # collinear

blocks.text: You might be tempted to compare slopes to decide turns, but the orientation test is strictly better.

items: No division, so no divide by zero on vertical lines
Exact with integer coordinates, avoiding floating point error
Handles every case with a single expression
Directly gives the three way answer you actually want

blocks.text: This primitive is reused throughout geometry.

items: Building a convex hull, keeping only the correct turns
Computing the signed area of a polygon
Testing whether a point lies inside a polygon

blocks.text: Nearly every geometry algorithm calls the orientation test somewhere inside it.
